name: Resection Planning and Margins
title: Resection Planning and Margins
answer: Resection planning and margins covers the work of deciding, before and during an operation, how much tissue to remove around a tumour and where the safe boundary lies. It sits inside surgical robotics and navigation, where imaging, tracking and robotic instruments meet the operating table. The topic spans preoperative planning from scans, intraoperative guidance that updates that plan as the surgeon works, and the pathology that later confirms whether the margin was clear. It matters most in cancer surgery of the breast, prostate, liver, lung and brain, where too little removed tissue risks leaving disease behind and too much removes function the patient needs.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Resection planning and margins covers the work of deciding, before and during an operation, how much tissue to remove around a tumour and where the safe boundary lies. It sits inside surgical robotics and navigation, where imaging, tracking and robotic instruments meet the operating table. The topic spans preoperative planning from scans, intraoperative guidance that updates that plan as the surgeon works, and the pathology that later confirms whether the margin was clear. It matters most in cancer surgery of the breast, prostate, liver, lung and brain, where too little removed tissue risks leaving disease behind and too much removes function the patient needs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on preoperative imaging, most often CT, MRI or ultrasound, plus a navigation system that registers those images to the patient's actual anatomy in the room. Optical or electromagnetic trackers follow instruments and patient position, and a robotic arm or a tracked probe carries the plan to the surgical field. Some systems add a console that overlays the planned margin on a live view, and some bring in intraoperative imaging or a specimen scanner to check the cut surface before the patient leaves. Computing is usually a workstation in the theatre suite rather than a distant data centre, because latency and network failure are not acceptable mid-operation.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Planning starts with segmentation of the tumour and nearby critical structures, which may be done by hand, by a trained model, or by a model with a human correcting the result. Registration then aligns the scan to the patient, and the surgeon reviews the proposed margin and adjusts it against anatomy, function and the planned approach. During the operation the navigation display shows instrument position relative to the plan, and the surgeon decides whether the margin looks adequate or needs widening. After removal, the specimen goes to pathology, where ink, slicing and microscopy give the definitive margin status, and that result is compared back to what the plan predicted. The loop is deliberately human in the middle, because the model proposes and the surgeon disposes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Responsibility for the margin sits with the operating surgeon, not with the software, and the plan is documented as a clinical decision with the imaging and model output that supported it. Devices used here generally need regulatory clearance as medical devices, and changes to a model or its intended use can trigger a new submission. Consent discussions should cover that computer guidance is being used and what happens if it is unavailable. Data governance covers patient imaging, which is identifiable and often shared with vendors for support or improvement, and procurement should settle where that data lives and how long it is kept. If a margin proves inadequate or a structure is injured, the record of what the system displayed becomes evidence, and the site's tracking of product liability litigation shows this is not a hypothetical concern.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward margins assessed in the room rather than days later, using fresh tissue imaging, rapid molecular methods and probes that sense residual disease on the cavity wall. Navigation is moving from a preoperative plan that ages during the operation to a model that updates as tissue shifts and is removed. Robotics and navigation are converging, so the same system that holds the instrument may also constrain the cut to the planned boundary. The open questions are validation, since a margin tool must be tested against pathology rather than against itself, and workflow, since any added step must earn its place in a busy theatre. Expect adoption to follow evidence and local commissioning rather than novelty.
